subject: business-studies

moments.title: The Wealth of Nations
moments.body: Smith publishes 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' on 9 March 1776. The opening chapters describe a pin factory: one worker alone can produce a handful of pins per day; ten workers, each specialised, produce 48,000 between them.

quote.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
quote.attrib: Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter II

moments.takeaway: Specialisation and exchange — not just hard work — explain the wealth gap between societies. The pin factory becomes the canonical example of division of labour in business teaching.

now.title: Smith in modern business
now.body: Smith's specialisation principle underlies every modern firm structure and supply chain. Globalised production extends division of labour across countries. Smith himself warned about the cognitive costs of extreme specialisation ('The man whose whole life is spent in performing a few simple operations... generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become').
now.open_questions: Where are the limits of specialisation in knowledge work, where general judgment matters more than narrow expertise?

reflection: Smith is invoked for free markets and forgotten for his warnings. The actual text is more cautious than its reputation.
